title: KV-temperature-gated tenanted preemptor for elastic continuous batching
creator: Aisha Karim
description:
Problem: Our current continuous-batching preemption heuristics are binary: when GPU memory pressure or latency budget breaches occur we interrupt slices and evict KV entries immediately. In mixed workloads this causes KV churn (hotset evictions followed by immediate reloads), transient latency spikes for tenants with hot context, and poor end-to-end SLO compliance for 99th-percentile tail latency.

Goal: Design and implement a tenanted, SLO-aware preemption policy that uses a lightweight per-tenant 'KV temperature' signal plus GPU memory pressure and per-request latency slack to drive graceful, incremental preemption and eviction. The policy should reduce KV thrash, preserve P99 latency for high-SLO tenants, and avoid large throughput regressions during compaction/eviction.

Key ideas:
- KV temperature: continuous per-tenant score (0..100) representing fraction of requests that hit hot KV entries over a sliding window + recency penalty. Higher score => hotter working set.
- Temperature gating: when preemption is considered, prefer preempting tenants with low temperature; for medium temperatures allow soft-yield windows rather than hard interrupts; for high temperature only allow non-evicting reclaim strategies (e.g., deferred compaction, checkpoint-to-host).
- Multistage eviction: rather than dropping entire KV slabs, perform small incremental checkpoints/trim steps with application-aware thresholds to limit transient miss-rate increase.
- Tenant-anchored reservations: allow minimal per-tenant KV reservation tokens to protect hot short-lived context (configurable by SLA tier).
- Latency slack budgeting: combine tenant SLO weight and per-request slack estimate to compute an interrupt cost budget; only preempt if cost budget positive and temperature gating allows it.

Why different: This approach shifts from global pressure heuristics to a tenanted, temperature-gated decision surface that reasons about both KV locality and SLO priority. It explicitly trades small throughput or memory overhead (reservations) for reduced miss-rate and tail latency.
acceptance_criteria: Implementation toggled behind runtime flag and feature-guard: kv_temperature_preemptor
On mixed synthetic workloads (hot and cold tenants) P99 generation latency for hot tenants increases by <= 10% compared to baseline without preemption under same load
KV miss-rate delta for hot tenants during preemption events <= 5%
Overall cluster throughput regression <= 3% during steady-state eviction operations
Memory fragmentation metric (percent free but unusable) reduced by >= 15% after incremental eviction vs. full-slab eviction in experiments
End-to-end e2e test harness & integration smoke tests added to ci/runtime-preemptor and passing
Dashboard panels for: per-tenant KV temperature, preemption decisions (reason tags), incremental eviction steps, and memory pressure timeline
notes: We must keep computational overhead low: temperature should be computed using existing request counters + an exponential decay window; avoid per-token counters.
Policy knobs to expose in console: reservation_size_per_tier, temperature_thresholds (cold/medium/hot), max_incremental_eviction_bytes, soft_yield_ms, preempt_cooldown_ms.
Trade-offs: reservations reduce reclaimable memory but avoid repeated reloads; incremental eviction increases background write/CPU load but smooths latency spikes.
Compatibility: Works on both Dedicated and Hosted runtimes. For Private deployments with strict KMS/HSM constraints ensure checkpointing path uses allowed temporary storage locations.

Security: checkpoint files may contain model KV fragments; retention policy must be short and encrypted-at-rest (integrate with KMS). Security review not required for MVP but flagged for release notes.
implementation_plan: Phase 1 (spike, 1 week): implement lightweight KV temperature probe and a simulated decision loop in a local runtime binary; run controlled microbenchmarks.
Phase 2 (prototype, 2 weeks): implement gating logic + incremental eviction API in runtime; add feature flag and unit tests.
Phase 3 (canary, 2 weeks): rollout to a single fleet slice with mixed-tenant synthetic traffic; capture dashboards and latency/miss metrics.
Phase 4 (rollout, 1 week): gradual ramp to remaining fleet slices, enable console knobs, and prepare runbook for rollback.
Phase 5 (cleanup): add documentation, update SDK behavior notes, and prepare an RFC for long-term policy evolution.
